title: The Spread - Mon 12 Oct 2026
notes:

The Spread - Monday, 12 October 2026

Top line: The Gulf tanker war widened over the weekend and crude rose. Brent hit $106.80, up $2.09, and WTI hit $93.78, up $1.93. Early Monday the Russia-Ukraine "energy ceasefire" had pulled prices lower, but the Middle East attacks outweighed it by the US session. European gas is at its highest since early 2023.

 Gulf: attacks spread beyond the Strait

What changed:
Tankers off Oman: A drone struck the tanker Petro Dolphin at Sohar Anchorage, off Oman, on Sunday. Two Indian seafarers are missing.
Tankers in the Strait: Another tanker was hit by a projectile while exiting Hormuz. gCaptain reports two more tankers struck inside the Strait.
US blockade: US forces disabled a cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman. Washington says the ship ignored warnings while trying to run its blockade of Iran.
Saudi Arabia: The Houthis hit King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with ballistic and cruise missiles on Saturday.
Talks: Iran's security chief called the US reply to Iran's seven conditions for reopening Hormuz "insufficient". There is no US comment in the items.

Transmission: Strikes now reach anchorages outside the Strait. That adds to Gulf loading and transit risk, and the risk premium is showing up in crude benchmarks. Freight is already stretched: Clarksons' ClarkSea index rose 12% in a week to a record $84,951/day. Possible knock-on: higher war-risk costs widen delivered-price gaps for medium-sour buyers in Asia.

Saudi position (claims, not verified flows):
At the WPC Energy Congress in Riyadh, Energy Minister Prince Abdulaziz said the kingdom's export capability is intact despite the attacks. No item gives export data to test this.
He also said Riyadh is looking to expand pipeline capacity to outlets outside the Gulf to 10 mb/d, within two to three years. That is a long-dated hedge, not near-term relief.

Outlook views:
BMI expects Brent to stay above $100 for months. It sees a US-Iran deal by end-Q1 2027 at the earliest.
Standard Chartered warns the market is mistaking adaptation for normalisation.

Diesel: The IEA says Hormuz is straining global diesel markets in particular and is coordinating with governments. France is releasing strategic reserves. TotalEnergies will cut French diesel and heating-oil prices further from 1 November.

 Russia: Trump's "energy ceasefire" and diesel deal

The claim: Trump said Sunday that Russia and Ukraine agreed to an energy ceasefire, effective immediately. Neither Moscow nor Kyiv confirms it in today's items. Rigzone separately reports Zelenskyy is on a collision course with Trump.

The diesel deal is under attack in Washington:
Republican Senator Thom Tillis said Trump's move to ease restrictions on Russian diesel may be illegal.
Republican Representative Brian Fitzpatrick plans to force a House vote on a bill blocking Russian oil purchases.

Context: Russian product exports reached a three-month high in September.

Transmission: If the truce holds, fewer strikes on Russian refineries would mean more exportable Russian diesel. That is bearish for diesel cracks, but with a lag while plants are repaired. For now the truce is one-sided and contested, and Monday's price action showed Gulf risk dominating.

Black Sea freight: Lukoil's Bulgaria manager says Black Sea oil-tanker insurance has risen from about $200,000 to $2.5 million per vessel. That is a single-source claim.

 European gas: TTF near €83

Price: Dutch TTF trades around €83/MWh, the highest since early

title: The Spread - Tue 13 Oct 2026
notes:
This episode is written with AI from public sources and read by an AI clone of Jaime's voice, not recorded by Jaime. Show notes link to every source.

The Spread - Tuesday, 13 October 2026

 Hormuz: six ships hit in one day
What changed: gCaptain now reports six commercial vessels struck in and around the Strait of Hormuz on 11 October: five tankers and a container ship. Our last edition carried two tankers hit inside the strait. The pace of attacks is rising, and the targets now include container shipping as well as tankers. Brent settled above $106 on Monday, in line with the $106.80 we reported yesterday.

Chain: more strikes on Gulf shipping → higher risk for owners lifting from the Gulf → freight that was already at record levels stays tight, and the supply-risk premium holds in Brent.

The items do not show how much Gulf crude and product export volume is actually lost. Tanker-tracking and loading data from Saudi and Iraqi terminals will show the scale.

 Houthis strike Riyadh's main airport
New front: Houthi attacks at the weekend hit Riyadh's main airport and caused deaths. gCaptain's analysis says this raises the risk of an escalation that draws in the US. That assessment is gCaptain's view, not a confirmed policy move.

Chain: the Houthis have now shown they can reach deep into Saudi Arabia → the risk premium covers Saudi assets as well as Gulf shipping. Possible knock-on: Yanbu exports on the Red Sea, the bypass route around Hormuz, come into scope if Houthi targeting widens. Today's items do not report any attack on Yanbu.

 LNG: Asia outbids Europe, coal gains
Gulf LNG flows are still more than 75% below their level before 28 February. The November European gas contract is trading above €81/MWh. Asian spot LNG has risen above European prices, which is pulling cargoes east. Coal is about 80% cheaper than LNG, and global coal demand is rising as a result.

Chain: Hormuz cuts Qatari and UAE LNG supply → Asian buyers outbid Europe for spot cargoes → Europe competes for fewer cargoes heading into winter, and buyers in both regions switch to coal where they can.

EU storage stood at 73.8% full on 11 October, up 0.14 points day on day. This revises the 73.7% we carried yesterday.

 Freight strands heavy crude in the Americas
High tanker rates have choked off exports of heavy crude from the Americas. At the same time, US refiners are running close to their limits, so the barrels are piling up in the region. US refinery utilisation was 92.7% in the week to 2 October.

Chain: record freight → the cost of shipping Americas heavy crude to distant buyers becomes prohibitive → heavy crude backs up at home, while US refineries have little spare capacity to absorb it. This is the reverse of the Hormuz problem: medium and heavy sour crude is scarce east of Suez but stranded in the Americas.

 Also noted
Japan: Trade Minister Ryosei Akazawa called for more oil stockpiling, closer cooperation between producer and consumer countries, and more infrastructure development in Asia. He did not give volumes or a timeline. https://www.rigzone.com/news/wire/japanurgesoilstockpilingdevelopment-12-oct-2026-184826-article/?rss=true
GPS interference: the UK Maritime and Coastguard Agency issued guidance note MGN 719. It warns that satellite navigation cannot be relied on in some busy shipping regions and tells crews to practise navigating without it. https://splash247.com/britain-urges-ships-to-prepare-for-life-without-reliable-gps/
Murphy Oil: reported an oil discovery offshore Vietnam, first oil at Lac Da Vang, and new production from its Chinook 8 well in the US Gulf. https://www.worldoil.com/news/20
